pages.name: Session 1 — First Light on the Trade Way

text.content:
Daggerford to the edge of the Misty Forest: the party takes the Trade Way south, avenges a slaughtered caravan at a bridge ambush, and claims a Dawnbringer's blade.

Setting Out from Daggerford

The campaign opened in the Silver Gauntlet, the adventurers' tavern at Daggerford's southern gatehouse — the party's last roof before the long road south. Over drinks, four travellers took each other's measure: Morgash the Gravemaker, orc fighter and ex–Flaming Fist caravan guard chasing one last big score; Gren Greenmantle, forest gnome sorcerer raised in the Misty Forest and outcast when his Spellfire surfaced — keeper of the party's map to the shards; Thomas A. Invictus, human paladin of Lathander and former scribe, whose murdered family set him hunting the Broken Heart; and Jetten Elisedil, wood elf ranger and Thomas's oldest friend, on the road to see him through it.

What the tavern's lore-swapping established: the green dragon in the rumors is likely young — perhaps a wyrmling; Shar is the goddess of loss, night, and forgotten memories, her faithful utterly secretive; and Greenrest is a small village nobody on the road knows much about. Before departing, Lord Hargrove opened the inn's vault and the party divided their stored gear — Morgash took up the Ember-Touched Greatsword, Gren the Wand of the War Mage +1, Thomas his +1 Shield and Cloak of Protection, Jetten the Quiver of Ehlonna and paired +1 Daggers — along with a thousand gold split four ways.

Travellers on the Trade Way

The road south offered its own small dramas. Two bickering "couriers," Pibb and Josk, asked the party to arbitrate a dispute about their horses — and Thomas, a scribe who knows every legitimate document-dealer in Daggerford, read Pibb instantly for a forger. Gren quietly interviewed the horses via Speak with Animals (well-rested, well-fed, no complaints). The duo huffed off north, unmasked but unhindered.

Later came Brother Tobin, a barefoot halfling priest of Chauntea, who blessed the party and pressed a Barley-Token on Jetten as a kindred spirit of the wilds — leaving a line worth remembering:

"The lady's been strange with her gifts of late. Some fields simply cannot fail; others starve a mile off. She doesn't usually play favorites."

The Bridge and the Cave

Late afternoon: an overturned merchant cart on a bridge, its wheel still spinning, crates picked over, fresh blood smeared toward the riverbank. Morgash picked many booted footprints out of the blood, and the trail led down to an unlit cave. Jetten scouted ahead in the dark and found a band of hobgoblins around a campfire — several wounded from their ambush, a big captain among them. The counsel was short. "We can't let them live," said Thomas. "They'll just attack whoever comes along the road next." Jetten's longbow opened the battle from the shadows.

It was a long, scrappy fight — a captain, warriors, archers, and a shaman with a poison vine staff who misty-stepped in from the deeper dark. Thomas's Bane ruined hobgoblin aim all night while Gren's Bless propped up the front line; Morgash chained Action Surge and Precision Attack through an ice-cold rolling streak ("Finally hit something. Finally!"); Thomas smote the captain and Jetten's arrow finished him from across the cave; Gren conjured a false cave wall with Minor Illusion and burned the shaman down with Scorching Ray from behind it. The last warrior, surrounded and staring down Gren's roared "Surrender or die!", dropped his sword. The interrogation yielded little — merchants were simply "the job" — and Jetten ended it with cold elven finality.

Aftermath — First Light

In the back chamber lay the hobgoblins' victims, dead barely an hour: two guards Thomas identified as paladins of Lathander — his own god — a high-elf merchant woman in fine Waterdhavian garb, and her human companion. Thomas prayed the psalm for the dead over the faithful and felt a warm wash of Lathander's approval. His knowledge of the road troubled him more: the Trade Way is normally safe. These hobgoblins seemed driven here from somewhere, scouring land they didn't know.

The captain's blade was no hobgoblin weapon: a rose-gold longsword, oddly warm, holding a little daylight even in the dark. Thomas felt a connection to it on sight, and attunement over the night's rest revealed First Light, a Dawnbringer's blade consecrated in a temple of Lathander — a +1 longsword carrying Heroism once per day. From the travellers' recovered chest the party also claimed a Driftglobe, a pouch of cut gems, an unread Traveller's Letter addressed to someone in Daggerford, a healer's kit, two casks of southern wine, a Potion of Healing, and 15 gp / 10 sp each. The victims were buried with last rites; the hobgoblins were not. The party long rested in a clean corner of the cave.

Where Things Stand

  • All four heroes stand at level 3. The next level comes with finding Greenrest. Shards held: 0 — each shard brings a level.
  • Morning of day two: to the east, the treeline of the Misty Forest. The map says leave the road here.
  • Greenrest still lies ahead — and nobody on the road knows much about it.
  • Unresolved: the Traveller's Letter (pocketed, unread), Brother Tobin's strange words about Chauntea's gifts, and whatever drove the hobgoblins onto the Trade Way.

pages.name: Session 2 — The Lure in the Mist

text.content:
East off the Trade Way and through the Misty Forest: the party fights off a blight ambush, follows a false light to an ettercap lair in a ruined elven temple, claims the scimitar Goldthorn — and reaches Greenrest at last, a picture-perfect village with one gray, dying tree at its heart.

Into the Misty Forest

Morning of day two. Thomas asked the party's one local about their destination — and Gren, raised in these woods, had never heard of Greenrest: Misty Forest settlements are small, secluded, and private, and a village unknown even to a forest gnome isn't strange here. Morgash hauled the wrecked cart off the road, and the company turned east into the trees. Jetten scouted ahead; Gren walked land he'd known all his life — and yet it was Morgash, the Baldur's Gate city orc on his first real woodland march, who kept picking the right trail while the ranger and the native second-guessed themselves. Nobody could explain it, including Morgash.

A Rest, Interrupted

Past midday the party stopped to rest in a clearing — and the birdsong stopped with them. Jetten and Gren both caught the warning signs in time, so when five blights (three twig, two vine) rose from the treeline and ringed the camp, nobody was surprised. Jetten's opening arrow killed a vine blight before it ever took a turn. Morgash cut a twig blight in half, then used his new Adrenaline Rush to dash across the clearing and block the far side. Thomas worked First Light's Sap mastery to spoil the blights' attacks, shrugged off an Entangle ("You will never be able to catch me"), and killed the last twig blight with a critical hit. Gren picked fire for his Sorcerous Burst on a hunch — the right call against dry wood. The fight ended without a single blight landing a blow. Gren's verdict: these things are a corruption of life itself, and somewhere out there is a source.

The Light That Beckoned

Hours later the mist gave way to a low gray cliff split by a cleft taller than a man — and a single small light hanging before it, warm as a candle but casting no glow and no shadow. It drifted toward them and back, beckoning. Gren wanted to help ("one of our fairy friends may be in distress"), so the party followed it in: cold air, wet stone, a sweet-rotten smell. Gren put his light cantrip on Thomas, and Jetten crept ahead — spotting the ambush in the webs before it could spring. "How delightful. It was a trap, guys." The light winked out.

The Web-Halls

The lair held a brood of ettercaps — and the night's best joke: Morgash, all-day navigator, rolled a natural 1 for initiative and went dead last. But he made the turn count when it came: the first ettercap kept stealing nervous glances at a closed door, and Morgash read it — he dashed across the hall and planted himself in front of that door before anything could come through. Jetten opened with shortsword and scimitar; Thomas cast Bless on the front line, which quietly paid off all fight. The first ettercap let out a wail — and reinforcements answered it. A broodling webbed Thomas in place; the Broodmother burst through the door Morgash was guarding, poisoned him with her bite — and got no further than the doorway he held. More broodlings came in along the walls and ceiling. On the lair's beat, the light came back hostile — a will-o'-wisp, striking with lightning out of invisibility and vanishing again before anyone could answer.

Gren burned the first ettercap down with Scorching Ray (two crits among them), then turned Subtle Spell + Magic Missile on the Broodmother — silent, unerring darts. Thomas cut himself free of the webbing, kept Morgash and Gren standing with Lay on Hands, and killed a broodling outright with a critical hit ("We're going to call you Thomas the Silent"). Morgash, twice poisoned at his post, cured himself twice from his jar of Keoghtom's Ointment and converted misses into hits with Precision Attack. Jetten's arrows wore the Broodmother down — and Gren's volley of Magic Missiles finished her. The will-o'-wisp escaped: it vanished after its last attack and never returned. Gren swore vengeance on it — "it, and all of its kind."

The Hidden Shrine

With the webs burned away, the lair turned out to be a ruined temple: worked stone, worn statues, etchings too old to read. Thomas's Religion check placed it — a shrine of the fey, likely elven, its bowls made for alms and water. Gren poured clean water into each empty bowl before they left. The bones scattered through the halls were picked clean. Down a south passage lay a more recent victim — a fey figure, months dead, a dagger still at its side — next to the hoard of everything the lights had lured in over the years. The gilded scimitar in that hoard pulled at Jetten the way First Light once pulled at Thomas; attuned overnight, it gave up its name:

Goldthorn — lost with its bearer to the webs of a hidden temple in the Misty Forest and dormant ever since, waiting on a worthy hand. Its fey magic stirs once between dawns: a bloom of clinging faerie light that lets nothing hide in shadow.

Stranger was a Dose of Greenrest Tonic — a stoppered clay vial of bitter green cordial, found among the web-wrapped effects of a traveller who never left the temple. The label, in a tidy, careful hand, reads only: "One swallow, seventh-day, as ever. — Selma." Thomas also spoke aloud what they learned of it: "Whoever drinks the swallow sleeps utterly, without dreams, for the next seven nights. No apothecary could name any other virtue… nor say why anyone would brew such a thing." The party long rested in the cleared temple, Jetten trancing on watch by the entrance.

First Sight of Greenrest

In the morning, two hours east, the trail climbed a final rise and the mist ended. Below, in green meadows under a clear sky: slate roofs around a square, straight chimney smoke, orchards and hedged fields, birdsong, cut hay — and an old stone watchtower on the height nearby. Greenrest, at last. One thing stands out: in the very center of the village, a single great tree gone gray and sickly — the one wrong note in an otherwise perfect song.

Where Things Stand

  • The party reaches level 4 — Greenrest found, milestone earned. Homework before next session: level up and choose your feat.
  • Spoils: Goldthorn (Jetten, attuned) · Cloak of Elvenkind (Jetten) · Lantern of Revealing & the Greenrest Tonic (Thomas) · Potion of Healing (Morgash) · 67 gp each.
  • Shards held: 0 — four shards of the Broken Heart to find; the choosing starts next session, down in the village (or up at the watchtower first).
  • Unresolved: the will-o'-wisp that escaped (Gren's sworn vendetta), the source of the blights, the dead fey bearer of Goldthorn, and why a village nobody has heard of brews a tonic against dreams.

August 11, 2026. Down the hill and into the warmest welcome money can't buy: a mayor who greets strangers like family, an inn that won't take a copper — and a town where nobody cries. A child's warning about black cats with too many legs, a night of borrowed grief nobody was supposed to dream, and a hunt that ends with the displacer pack dead in the ruins where the Kestrel Company fell.

The Warmest Welcome

At the trailhead above town, Morgash found tracks circling the path where it leaves the forest — an animal, or animals, with a gait no one could count legs for — every print turning back into the trees. Whatever walks that circle does not enter Greenrest. The party went down anyway, into orchards and full fields, and were met in the square by Mayor Oswin Applewhite, who welcomed them like family coming home. The tour was long and generous: the Long Rest and its barman Ambrose, the smithy, the church of the Earth Mother, the brew house, Selma's apothecary, the docks, the Full Larder, the Hedgewatch garrison — and the mayor's own tower on the hill, because the mayor always lives above the town; it's tradition. Rooms, meals, and ale: free. Asked about the Broken Heart, Oswin allowed that another company — the Kestrel Company — came asking the same questions some months back, got directions and full supplies, and never came back. Asked whether anyone here weeps over anything, the mayor smiled: "There is no crying here."

Pip and the Black Cats

The best intelligence in Greenrest was a halfling child on the inn porch. Pip — taller than Gren, as he made sure Gren knew — admired Gren's Minor Illusion of a green dragon, declined a gold piece because he already has everything he needs, and then asked the question the adults don't: "Did the black cats follow you too?" Big black cats, too many legs, circling the town when the Kestrels were here — and again, an hour before this party walked out of the trees. He never told anyone, because he didn't want to bother them. Jetten put a name to it: displacer beasts, fey predators that stalk their prey.

Provisions and Suspicions

Mother Wend at the Full Larder knew all four names before they crossed her threshold. The party emptied most of its shared gold into her shelves: Gauntlets of Ogre Power for Thomas, Bracers of Archery for Jetten, a Wand of Magic Missiles for Gren — and Thomas passed his Stone of Good Luck to Gren to make the attunement work. At the garrison, Constable Warrenholt gave it to them straight: his scouts say the beasts stalked the Kestrel Company, waited until the company limped home spent, and killed them at an old temple southeast of town — and such creatures never abandon a hunt while their quarry lives. His advice: pick the moment yourselves, go at full strength, and kill them first. And at the inn, the gravedigger Coll said quietly that something hasn't felt right since the Kestrels came through — they complained of bad dreams, the way he had bad dreams as a boy, before Selma "helped him." The whole town, it seems, drinks the dreamless tonic every seventh day, from childhood on. And Thomas already carries proof: his own Dose of Greenrest Tonic, the stoppered clay vial found in the hidden temple among the web-wrapped effects of a fey wanderer who never left it. He read its label to the party again:

"One swallow, seventh-day, as ever. — Selma."

The same seventh-day cadence Coll had just described. Gren made the call for everyone: "Let's spend the night without drinking the tonic. Something's fishy about this town."

The Night Without the Tonic

All four dreamed the same visitor: a beautiful, pale woman standing on a hill, her hair the leaves and branches of a white tree, weeping. Her grief was not a picture they watched — it poured into each sleeper and found the grief already living there.

  • Thomas stood on the hill with her and was pulled back to the murder of his wife and children — how lonely he is, how they are gone from the mortal world forever and can never be gotten back. He took his Oath of Vengeance over that wound; in the dream there was no vengeance in him at all. Only grief.
  • Morgash dreamed first of Baldur's Gate: the day he pledged his love to Lae'zel, the fiery githyanki warrior, and her answer — "I cannot love someone in this world. I must go fight and destroy my queen… Goodbye, my Morgash. I will remember you" — before she leapt onto a red dragon and vanished into the dark sky. Then the sky went hazy, and he stood before the tree-woman feeling nothing but the loneliness of being left.
  • Gren saw her white and glowing and sad, and her sadness became the day the elders of his Misty Forest village asked him to leave. They called it "going to explore the world" — but in the dream he finally asked the question underneath: did they send him away because of the spellfire inside him? Because he was different? Cast out, unwanted, unloved — and still loving his village with all his heart.
  • Jetten should not dream in trance at all — but he did, eyes open, his moonstone necklace glowing bright green the whole while. He sat with the loss of his sister, dead so long ago, and the particular cruelty of an elf's long life: he goes on for centuries, hers was cut short, and no stretch of his years will hand hers back.

Four sleepers, four separate griefs — one weeping woman in all four dreams. In the morning, three laid it out plainly; Morgash admitted the woman and kept the rest: "I won't give details about my broken heart."

The Dryad and the Gray Tree

Gren's temple schooling surfaced word-perfect, and Thomas's studies agreed: the woman is a dryad — a fey being who lives an immortal life passing between the shape of an elf and the shape of a tree. Thomas said the obvious out loud: the one gray, dying thing in this flourishing town is a tree. In the square they found it under guard — four soldiers, on standing orders from the mayor and the constable, to let no one harm it and let no one so much as chip the bark. It has "always been this way": the one thing in Greenrest that doesn't flourish, watched like a treasure. "Life is not perfect," Morgash told the party flatly, in the middle of the perfect town.

The Hunt at the Kestrel Camp

Southeast on the constable's trail to a ruined temple where the road ends: a cold firepit, scattered bones, a chest, a brush pile — the Kestrel Company's last camp. Jetten's eyes found the watcher in the fog long before it wanted to be found. He opened like a Gloom Stalker — Dread Ambusher for an extra arrow, Hunter's Mark on the beast. The shot flew perfect. It missed anyway: Displacement kept the beast's true body a step from where it seemed to stand. It howled — and the ambush turned inside out. Two more beasts broke from the bramble, and behind them came the alpha, half again their size. The party was encircled.

The first rounds were a beating. Gren's Shatter caught two beasts square — Avoidance, and neither was scratched. A rend put Jetten in the dirt; a tentacle beat him unconscious; Gren's Cure Wounds through Subtle Spell stood him back up, Spellfire Burst wrapping Morgash in bolstering flames. Morgash needed them — he had closed with Adrenaline Rush, been raked to nothing, and Relentless Endurance refused the fall. He stood at the brink, drank potion after potion, caught his Second Wind, and killed the first beast with a Precision Attack backhand. Jetten tried the textbook counter — Faerie Fire, to paint the beasts in light no illusion could hide — and the beast in the cube twisted out of the save untouched. A tentacle crit left Thomas one hit from the dark and broke his Bless — so the paladin reached for scholarship instead of steel: the Lantern of Revealing, unhooded, did what the spell couldn't and tore the displacement off the pack. The beasts shrieked, then learned, and played the edge of the glow while Thomas laid Bane on one — every strike it threw afterward fell short — and swore a Vow of Enmity against another.

Then the tide turned. Thomas landed First Light and rode it with a Thunderous Smite — thunder cracked across the ruin, the beast flew backward through Morgash's reach, and the orc's opportunity strike killed it in the air. Jetten worked Goldthorn and his +1 dagger in a Nick-mastery weave, Hunter's Mark riding every hit, every freed bonus action a Healing Word. Gren leaned on Magic Missile — wand, then slots, volley after volley — flicked up Shield against the alpha's claws, re-laid Bless with his Fey-Touched casting, and staggered the alpha with an upcast five-dart burst. Thomas met it: First Light through the alpha's chest, Lathander's light bursting from the wound. The last beast fled leaderless into the forest and did not return.

What the Kestrels Left

The camp gave up the company's story in objects: a crate stamped by Greenrest's own Full Larder — preserves, a silver kestrel locket, a charcoal sketch of a weeping woman, a purse of gold, and Marn's journal beside Sera's map of the four ruins — and a brush pile hiding their arms: Sera's bow and blades, Marn's crossbow, Brakk's plate armor rent through by great claws, a quiver of enchanted arrows, a mighty Maul of Momentum, and a Pearl of Power. All of it went to the party stash; the journal and map wait to be read in safety. Thomas, staring at the larder-stamped crate: "I'm very suspicious of that town. They've given away all this stuff for free." The party walked back down into Greenrest for a safe night's rest — this time with nothing hunting them on the road home.

Where Things Stand

  • The displacer pack is broken — two beasts to Morgash, the alpha to Thomas; one fled leaderless into the forest.
  • Spoils: Gauntlets of Ogre Power (Thomas) · Bracers of Archery (Jetten) · Wand of Magic Missiles (Gren) · Stone of Good Luck passed to Gren · the Kestrel camp haul in the party stash, Maul of Momentum with Morgash.
  • Unread: Marn's Journal and Sera's Map of the Four Ruins — the Kestrel Company's own words and route.
  • Known: the dream-woman is a dryad; the guarded gray tree is the town's one imperfection; the whole town drinks Selma's dreamless tonic weekly from childhood — and the party has chosen to keep dreaming.
  • Shards held: 0 — and the first ruin is chosen: the caves, where the townsfolk once pointed the Kestrel Company. Selma's apothecary still waits for its visit.

pages.name: Session 4 — The Heart Under the Hill

text.content:
August 18, 2026 — The party skips the road home and goes straight down into the caves: a catacomb cut five hundred years ago by three treasure hunters who found something warm and beating and could not put it down. Five wights fall. The first shard of the Broken Heart comes up out of the dark.

Breaking Camp

The Kestrel Company's last camp made a serviceable staging ground, and the spoils finally got sorted. Gren claimed the Pearl of Power and returned the Periapt of Wound Closure to the party stash; Jetten took the quiver of silver-banded arrows; Morgash bound himself to the Maul of Momentum. Then they spread out Sera's Map of the Four Ruins and argued about where to go. Marn's journal had already told them what waited under the caves, and Morgash made the argument that carried: the Kestrels never got past the dead, so whatever they were hunting is probably still down there — and this time the party knows what is coming. They slept at the camp, and in the morning went southeast instead of home.

A Stair Cut for Nobody's God

The trail ended at a squat stone minaret pushing up out of the forest floor, a staircase winding down inside it. Gren consulted a squirrel first, and got exactly what a squirrel gives you: "That's not where food is. There are weird sounds. We don't go down there." He set a Light on the sun symbol of Thomas's shield and they descended.

At the bottom stood a figure carved from living rock — robed, taller than a man, worn past all recognition. No face. No hands. A shallow offering basin at its feet, and a skeleton on the floor impaled on spikes jammed into the stone long after the place was built. Thomas's scholarship gave the party more than they wanted: five centuries old without a scratch, and belonging to no faith he knew. No holy symbols, no scripture, no iconography of any living god. The chisel strokes were too small and too many for any tool still in use — the work of people with nothing but time. Whoever cut this was not following a tradition. They were inventing one. And the offering basin had never once been used.

The Empty Coffins

A skeleton came down the corridor at Morgash and the fighting started. Jetten painted the crypt in Faerie Fire; Morgash closed with an Adrenaline Rush, took a miss, and shattered the thing with a Riposte. Thomas's javelin and Jetten's bow cleared the rest. Then the party opened every coffin set into the walls and found all of them empty. Gren said a prayer over each anyway. Jetten put it shorter: "Let the dead lie."

Aldous

The next door opened on zombies and something upright and clearly dead standing in the middle of them. It pointed a sword and said "You will join us." Gren opened his Innate Sorcery and burned it with Scorching Ray; it came on through Jetten's Entangle anyway and cut Morgash with a blade sheathed in cold green light. Then it reached out one hand — "Join me" — and something worse than a wound happened. The gash closed. What was underneath it did not.

Thomas ended it with First Light. And what they found on the body changed the temperature of the night: a bronze Kestrel Company locket at its throat, and a sword so cold Gren refused to touch it bare-handed. Marn's journal had the name and the sentence both:

"Aldous's wounds closed, but he did not mend. Edda would not leave him."

The same words the party had just watched happen to Morgash. Thomas raised his holy symbol and prayed over the man. Nobody suggested resting in the tomb after that. Before they moved on, Gren showed the others the acorn his village elders pressed into his hand the day they sent him away — taken from the heart-oak of his warren, still green after all these years, to be planted the day he finds where he belongs. "I still have not found the place where I belong."

The Keeper's Seat

A long pillared hall, and on a platform at the far end a wight seated on a throne who raised a hand and beckoned them in. He answered questions, which was more than the last one did. Asked what had become of Aldous's companion: "She's here. She's with us. She's happier." Thomas asked the only question he had — why shouldn't we destroy you here and now — and the throne answered with the line that ended the parley:

"I thought you would be interesting. But your insolence irritates me. You will not make a suitable wight — you'll make an excellent zombie."

Jetten's first arrow dropped the archer before the line even formed. Then Edda — a caster, exactly as Marn's journal implied — locked Jetten rigid with Hold Person. Morgash went at her: a miss dragged home with a Precision Attack, a Topple that put her flat, and when she held the spell anyway, an Action Surge that broke it. Jetten came unstuck mid-stride.

Osric spent the fight taking Morgash apart from the inside — the same reaching hand every exchange, another piece of him each time. The orc kept standing. Thomas laid Bane across the platform and worked First Light with Sap. And then Gren solved the room: he opened the Driftglobe and chose daylight. The chamber went white, and Osric and Edda shrieked and shrank from it, and for the rest of the fight nothing the dead swung came in straight. The skeletal mage smothered the globe under a sphere of Darkness — so Gren walked over, picked the sun up in one hand, and carried it back out of the dark.

After that it was arithmetic. Edda's Command slid off Morgash and his maul answered, and she went down beside the man she would not leave. Asked how he wanted to finish the Keeper, Thomas did not hesitate. The head went up, came down, and rolled all the way down the dais stairs.

Hesper, Who Was Tired

Through the east doors: another wight, flanked by two zombies, standing over a stone slab with chains on it. She waved the zombies still before anyone drew, looked at the blood on the party, and worked it out for herself — "You came through the crypts. That means Osric is finally dead, or you would not be standing in that doorway." Then, almost kindly: "He was very old and very tired. I hope he was courteous with you. He doesn't suffer insolence well."

"I am Hesper. I will answer plainly. No need for riddles, no need for bargaining. To be honest, I haven't even talked to anyone in a very long time. What is your question?"

They asked, and she told them everything in the flattest voice imaginable. She was the mortician; she prepared the wights. And five centuries ago — she was not sure of the number and did not much care — she and Osric and Cadoc had been treasure hunters.

"We found a glowing shard in a cave. It was warm, beating, the size of two cupped hands. We saw it; we couldn't put it down. We brought it here to keep it safe. After time, our greed turned into undeath. We cut the stair so no one else could take it. We cut every way in that we knew. And so we stood with the Graveheart — lonely — but it gave us life. It's here, guarded by Cadoc, waiting for the next body to be prepared as a wight to keep us company."

That was the whole of it, with no defence offered: three friends who found something they could not put down and stayed with it until staying was all they were. The room the party was standing in was where new company got made. She warned them there would be no bargaining with Cadoc, who was closest to the heart and furthest gone. She told them to take what was in her chest — a bone key for the locked west doors, and a stoppered flask warm to the palm the way the shard is warm. And then she asked.

"But I'm tired. I don't want to do this anymore."

Gren asked her how she would like it done. She walked to the slab where she had prepared so many others and laid her head down on it. The party gave her what she asked for, and in the same instant both zombies fell where they stood, as if someone had let go of a string. There was one flask and three men carrying holes in them; Morgash drank it and the cold went out of him. For Thomas and Gren the answer was less kind but at least it was an answer — one full night's sleep in a real bed, not a dungeon, and the wounds close on their own.

The Guardian

The bone key turned and the last room was waiting with its lights already on: a heap of dead piled up the far wall with red points burning in their eye sockets, an altar, and a hooded figure holding a scythe wrapped in fire that gave no heat. Behind him, mounted in a container, a great crystalline heart.

Cadoc moved first and he was fast. As Thomas crossed the floor, the guardian simply opened a hand toward him from across the chamber and the dark between them caught like oil on water. Thomas took the worst of the night from a man who never moved his feet. Morgash burned an Adrenaline Rush to reach him, forced a miss home with a Precision Attack, put him on his back with a Topple, and hit him again on an Action Surge. Thomas kept the scythe off true with Sap and spent his last spell slot on a Divine Smite that burned all the brighter for what Cadoc was. Gren, down to scraps, lit him up with a Guiding Bolt for whoever swung next.

The skeletal mage fought dirty to the end and finally put Morgash on the floor — where Relentless Endurance caught him a hair above nothing. He got up into the middle of five enemies who all wanted him specifically. Cadoc swung the burning scythe at him and fumbled it badly, and that was the end: Morgash's Riposte came back through the gap and the maul followed it down.

What Jetten Saw

They stood in a room lit by its own dead, and the Graveheart sat in front of them — a great crystal heart, arterial red going to violet in the deep of it. Jetten reached out and took it, and it showed him something.

The pieces scatter into the dark, hardening as they fly. The burst drives the mists back all around her in a great ring, baring a green valley beside a beautiful lake. And where she stood: a tree. Gray. Lifeless. Asleep.

Then one faint heartbeat. And it is over.

"Oh, it's the mighty warlord of the wood! All of the squirrels throughout the entire forest know of the great Gren."

They paid him proper obeisance, told him the big green one sleeps on the shiny warm thing at the far end and the water is bad, and went in with him to guard him. Pudgy squeezed through a rockfall no person could pass and came back delighted: there's a hallway on the other side. You are a mighty Gren. How did you know?

The Drowned Temple

Behind a carved door, a Shambling Mound lurched out of the dark. Morgash's maul knocked it flat twice, a Riposte answered its whip of a tendril, Invictus bashed it down again, and Jetten's shortsword went through it until it crumbled at his feet.

Beyond the next doors waited a horned, tiefling-looking druid with eyes glowing an unearthly green — must serve the master — and a giant crocodile. The crocodile clamped its jaws on Invictus; still in its mouth, he slammed his shield into its snout and cut it twice, and when it bit him again his Death Armor killed it. Jetten put a perfect Dreadful Strike into the druid and dropped him with the next arrow. Pudgy scratched the last locked door open, a lever in a room of old pulleys lifted the bar from the great doors, and the party drank their potions.

Bramblemaw

The doors opened on a long causeway across still green water, crocodiles drifting below, and the dragon at the far end. Come for my treasure, eh? You'll die instead.

He breathed first. A wall of poison rolled down the stones, and Pinenut, Honeysuckle and Pudgy, right behind Gren as they had promised, did not come out of it.

Then four rounds of the hardest fighting the party has done. Invictus Misty Stepped straight into the dragon's face and smashed him to the stones with his shield. Bramblemaw reached into Jetten's mind with Mind Spike and dropped him; Gren's Healing Word had him back up at once. Legendary Resistance shrugged off a second shield bash and Gren's Slow. Morgash got close, and the Maul of Momentum's Topple took the dragon's legs out from under him — and Action Surge kept the blows coming. The dragon dropped Invictus with his mind; Gren brought him back and sang the Wand of Magic Missiles into the dragon; a Counterspell was brushed aside. The second breath put Jetten and Invictus down together.

Morgash poured Selma's potion down Invictus's throat and hauled him back, then knocked the dragon flat again and swung until the maul sizzled with light. Invictus spent two small points of Lay on Hands to stand Jetten up. The dragon's best strike of the night left Gren standing on almost nothing.

"This is for Honeysuckle, Pinenut and Pudgy, you son of a—"

Careful Spell. Fireball. The dragon twisted away from the worst of it, and it did not matter. The fire took Bramblemaw and he did not get up. Freed of his hold, the crocodiles swam off into the dark water.

The Thornheart

Behind a door to the north lay a glowing green heart, and Invictus picked it up.

A quarter of a heart, turned to crystal: venom green, bright and vivid and faintly poisonous-looking, the size of two cupped hands… It is warm — warmer than the air — and it beats, slowly, faintly… It is the exact green of the dragon that hoards it, which is either a coincidence or isn't — and the Wyrmwood has grown briar around it the way a body grows scar tissue.

Holding it showed him the green woman weeping, her heart bursting, and a grey, leafless tree where she had stood. Once between dawns, it can raise the dead. Gren wanted to raise Pudgy on the spot — his only worshipper, practically his head priest. Invictus asked instead which heart could bring back his family, and learned that only the whole one could — if the four pieces are ever joined, at the source, at the tree.

And Invictus said the thing nobody else was ready to hear: "I already know the answer, because this sword has been whispering to me."

Where Things Stand

  • All four shards are in hand — the Graveheart (Morgash), the Tideheart (Gren), the Duskheart (Jetten) and now the Thornheart (Invictus): advantage on Dexterity saves, and once between dawns it casts raise dead.
  • The heart can be made whole — together, at the source. The choice of whether to do it is next.
  • Bramblemaw is dead. His hoard is the party's: a Staff of Withering, a Decanter of Endless Water, another Driftglobe, a Rival Coin found Tiamat side up, and a fortune in gems.
  • Pudgy, Honeysuckle and Pinenut lie in the dragon's hall. The Thornheart could raise one of them, for a few more dawns.
  • Greenrest is awake. The whole town dreamed the breaking, the tonic has failed, the elders are meeting, and the children play at it outside the inn.
  • Invictus says his sword already knows what should be done.

Tuesday, 29 September 2026 — the last session. A squirrel raised, a sword refused and buried, the whole town dreaming, three mobs held off in the square, and four hearts returned to the tree. The Dreamer went free, and the paladin remembered his name.

A Heartbeat for Pudgy

In the quiet after Bramblemaw, Invictus pressed the Thornheart to the little grey body of Pudgy, and green light threaded into it like new roots. The temple squirrel shook, looked up, and asked the only question that mattered: "Did we kill the dragon? Did we beat him?" Gren told him yes, and that Honeysuckle and Pinenut had not made it, and promised to bury them outside. The party rested in the geased druid's old camp south of the great hall.

The Duskheart Speaks

In the grey morning Jetten's eyes turned ink-black. The Duskheart had gone cold against his chest, and his hand closed around it without his asking. The voice was his; the words were Shar's, and Midnight glowed in its sheath while he spoke:

"Invictus. Killing my high priest was regrettable, but it is forgivable. My offer still stands. Take the heart shards and Midnight to the Dreamer's tree. Find the tree's heart knot, and plunge the blade into it. Midnight will drain the power from the tree and the shards. The Dreamer will be trapped. Each shard can grant you a resurrection, and the heart of the tree will grant you a fifth. The shards will be dead, but Midnight will have the ability to give you your five resurrections. You will win. You will get your family back. The town will win. The Dreamer's summer will remain in Greenrest forever. I will win. My will shall be done. Think carefully, Invictus. This is my last offer."

Invictus did not dismiss it. One fae against a whole town living well on her captivity; the pain of his loss gone strangely easy to bear — "I think that's what Shar does for her acolytes." His friends answered him one by one. Jetten called it a bargain with the devil. Morgash would not let him pretend: "It's not the same sword. Don't lie to yourself." Jetten reminded him the sword had once been called First Light, and he found he did not remember. Gren told him he had done nothing wrong and needed no redemption — "but if you do this, you will need redemption." In the end Invictus leaned on them, and refused.

The Dawnfather in the Fog

On the lakeshore at dawn he knelt with his psalter, held the black sword up to the sky, and begged Lathander to take Shar's power out of him. The fog curled away, and the Dawnfather appeared across the water:

"You are not completely lost, my child, but the sword you wield must be left here. Bury it. First Light is gone."

They buried Midnight on the shore together, and Pudgy swore never to tell where ("What is? I don't know anything. Yes, sir."). Honeysuckle and Pinenut were laid to rest beneath a tree heavy with acorns. Jetten gave Invictus a plain scimitar to carry in the dead sword's place, and they left quickly: he could hear the buried blade calling to him.

The Fourth Dream

As they crossed into Greenrest, Jetten's moonstone glowed green, and all four were standing in the dream again.

  • The hill — bare, the fog close, the tree where she had always stood.
  • The town — all of Greenrest was there in their nightclothes, and no mist hid anyone now: Oswin, Selma, Enid, Ambrose, Warin, even little Pip.
  • The Dreamer — for the first time she looked straight at them. She had forgiven Corin, and herself, and she asked to be set free: "Bring the hearts to my tree. Find the heart knot. Place them in it, one by one, and I will absorb them. On the fourth, I shall be free. Please, help me. I've been trapped for centuries."
  • Invictus — as she faded, she looked at him last, and smiled a little.
  • Jetten — his moonstone carried them in, and glowed the whole time.

They woke at the edge of town, and Invictus spoke first: "My vote is to go straight there and do it."

The Mayor in the Road

Oswin was waiting near the square, out of breath, with Pip beside him. He had seen them in the dream. He offered a key to the city, a home, free meals, anything; the fog would come back, the town would never prosper again. Invictus answered that it was evil to keep her trapped, and Pip looked up at the mayor: "I think he's right, Mayor. They need to do what they need to do." Oswin gave in, promised to stand the guards down, and went to tell the elders.

The Heart Knot

The word did not reach everyone. Three crowds came down on the square with pitchforks, clubs, torches and buckets of vegetables. Each heart had to be set in the knot one at a time, a full turn apiece. Gren's Hypnotic Pattern froze the biggest crowd for the whole fight. Invictus boomed a warning with Thaumaturgy, and Morgash's Tactical Mind carried his over the line; the mobs hesitated for a round. Jetten set the Duskheart. Entangle pinned the torchbearers; Morgash set the Graveheart; a cabbage bounced off Gren's Shield. Invictus called a celestial horse with Find Steed; Gren set the Tideheart while tomatoes flew; Morgash's pike answered two missed pitchforks with Riposte. Then Invictus leaned far out of the saddle and pressed the Thornheart into the knot — "Blot out all my iniquities, Lathander" — and kept his seat through a tomato to the eye.

The Passing

On the fourth heart the knot opened, and the dryad stepped out holding the whole heart. "It's stone. It has been stone in your hands for so long, warm and hard. And now it beats inside of me again." In her hands it lost its edges and went soft and warm, and it was not a jewel at all: a plain, red, ordinary heart. She took it back, the tree burst into full bloom, and she was gone. From far off came her voice — "Thank you. I can never repay you" — and Morgash's reply: "Yes, you can. Wait." The mob drifted away, beaten. Pudgy trotted up the street, heard the news, took an acorn, and decided to stay by Gren for good.

The Mist Comes Home

The mists began to roll back into the valley. The townsfolk would not look at them; the elders understood and could not forgive; Oswin asked them, quietly, to go. And the paladin stopped short: "Thomas. My name is Thomas."

After

  • Greenrest. Leaves fell in the square for the first time in living memory, and the children played in them. A few families went south. But at a sick child's bedside Enid prayed, and for the first time something answered. The harvests would be smaller, but real, and the town had a healer of its own.
  • Morgash. The dragon's gems were his big score. He stayed anyway, to hold the gate at Hedgewatch — "I feel responsible" — and in time was forgiven, with free meals from Oswin and a room at the Full Larder for good.
  • Jetten. His moonstone glowed green one last time, and he dreamed of his sister, a true dream sent by the Dreamer, and said goodbye. In the morning the stone was milky white.
  • Thomas. In Daggerford he made peace with the temple of Lathander, read every name on his family's five graves aloud, and then his own. His grief ended. Then he and Jetten went wandering together, slaying evil wherever they found it.
  • Gren. The squirrels spread the name of Gren the Mighty, who freed the Green Lady, and the warren called him home to a feast. He came back to Greenrest, planted his Everseed Acorn beside the old tree, and stayed — with Pudgy as the squirrels' prophet. He, Morgash and Pudgy became the Three Amigos, and his old debt to Morgash is paid in acorns by the orc's bed every morning.

The Broken Heart of Greenrest is complete. All four finish at level 6.
